desc:
A wallet holds counts[i] coins of value coins[i] for every index i. The coin values are distinct and there is no divisibility pattern between them.

Return the fewest coins from the wallet that add up to exactly amount, or -1 if it cannot be done. An amount of 0 needs 0 coins.

coins = [1,5], counts = [2,3], amount = 12 -> 4   (5+5+1+1)
coins = [1,5], counts = [2,3], amount = 17 -> 5   (5+5+5+1+1)
coins = [3,4], counts = [1,1], amount = 6  -> -1
constraints: 1 ≤ coins[i] ≤ 1,000 and all values are distinct
hints: With unlimited coins this is the classic coin change. What breaks if you reuse that DP unchanged?

A coin with count k can be taken 0..k times. You could try every number of copies, but there is a faster way: write k as a sum of pieces 1, 2, 4, ..., plus a remainder, so every number 0..k is a sum of some of the pieces.
Turn each piece (t copies of value c) into one 0/1 item of weight t * c and cost t. Run the 0/1 knapsack minimum best[s] = min(best[s], best[s - w] + t) with s going downward, and read best[amount].
editorial: Splitting a supply of k identical coins into pieces of sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., 2^(m-1) and a final remainder r = k - (2^m - 1) lets every count from 0 to k be formed as a sum of a subset of the pieces, and no larger count can be formed. Each piece of t copies behaves like one item that weighs t * c and costs t coins, to be taken or left whole.

That turns the problem into a 0/1 knapsack with 'minimum cost for exactly this weight': best[s] = min(best[s], best[s - w] + t), iterating s downward so each piece is used at most once, with best[0] = 0 and everything else infinite. There are O(n · log k) items, so the time is O(n · log k · amount). The answer is best[amount], or -1 if it is still infinite.
